notes: Criterion 7: 'Then some figures came to it.' A beginner does not know 'figures' in this sense, but the next sentences explain it. Optional fix: 'Then some strange beings came to it.' or 'Then some strange people came to it.'
Criterion 7: 'Hours went by.' The phrasal verb is easy to work out from context. Optional: 'Many hours passed.'
'Elstead wanted to see the ocean bottom.' would read more naturally as 'Elstead wanted to see the bottom of the ocean.' (this also matches quiz Q1).
'Elstead was well.' Optional: 'Elstead was OK.' This is a style choice.
'At last, Elstead came out into the night air.' Elstead is still inside the sphere here. Clearer: 'At last, the sphere came out into the night air.'
'Every house in it gave light' is a little odd. Suggest 'Every house in it was full of light'.
No passives or conditionals found. 'thick enough to stand the great weight of the water' is fine, though 'to hold back' would be a bit clearer for B1 readers.
'their enormous eyes had been formed for a world without sunlight' is slightly stiff. Suggest 'their enormous eyes seemed made for a world without sunlight'.
'The Ptarmigan rode at anchor' is unlikely in water five miles deep and hundreds of miles from the coast. Suggest 'The Ptarmigan lay motionless on a sea so calm...'.

summary: All five levels faithfully retell Wells's 'In the Abyss': the steel sphere with its lead weight and clockwork release, the long wait and the midnight return, the luminous fish, the upright big-eyed deep-sea people, the city of lights and the worship of the sphere, the release in the middle of the ceremony, and Elstead's second descent with no return. Grammar fits each level, every quiz key is correct and unambiguous, and the content suits a 4+ rating. Only minor wording notes remain.
